On Tuesday morning, Bodie Aldwick arrived at school early and found the courtyard full of noise. A mother duck was walking in circles near the bench, and eleven small ducklings were following her. The courtyard had walls on all four sides, and the only way out was through the school building.

Mr. Beckford, the caretaker, came out with a cup of tea. "She nests here every spring," he said. "The pond is behind the gym, but the ducklings are too small to fly over the wall."

Bodie wanted to pick up the ducklings and carry them to the pond in a box. Mr. Beckford shook his head. "If we take them, she may leave them," he said. "We'll make a path for her instead."

Together they opened the doors of the long hallway that led to the gym. Mr. Beckford put chairs on both sides to make a narrow road. Then they stood far back and waited quietly.

For ten minutes the mother duck only watched. At last she stepped into the hallway, and the ducklings hurried after her in a tight line. She walked past the classrooms, through the gym and out the back door. Bodie counted the ducklings as they reached the grass by the pond. There were eleven.

At lunch, Bodie told the whole class what had happened. The next spring, Bodie was the first student to offer to help.

Few birds put their heads through as much as woodpeckers do. To reach insects hidden under bark, to carve out holes for their nests and to send signals to other woodpeckers, they hammer their beaks against wood, sometimes more than ten times a second. Each strike ends in an abrupt stop, and the forces involved are far greater than those that would leave a person dizzy or injured. For a long time, the obvious question was how the birds manage to keep their brains safe.

The usual answer was that the woodpecker's head works like a shock absorber, a device that soaks up the energy of a blow so that less of it reaches whatever lies behind. Writers pointed to the spongy bone in the bird's skull and to a long, thin bone attached to the tongue, which curves around the back of the head and was thought to act like a safety belt. The idea was so widely accepted that engineers studied woodpeckers when designing helmets and protective cases for delicate equipment.

A few years ago, a team of biologists decided to test the idea directly. Instead of examining skulls in a laboratory, they filmed living woodpeckers of three different species with high-speed cameras while the birds pecked. By tracking points on the beak and near the eye, they could measure how quickly each part of the head slowed down at the moment of impact. If the skull were absorbing shock, the area around the brain should have slowed down more gently than the tip of the beak.

In the films, the beak and the braincase stopped almost together, which meant the head behaved less like a cushion and more like a stiff hammer. The researchers then used computer models to ask what a cushion would actually do. The answer was surprising: a head that absorbed shock would waste much of the energy of each strike, so the bird would have to hit far harder to break the same amount of wood. For an animal that can peck thousands of times a day, that would be a poor trade.

If the head is a hammer, why is the brain safe? The team's answer lies in size. A small brain is far less affected by a sudden stop than a large one, because the pressure that builds up inside a brain during an impact depends partly on its size. According to their calculations, the forces of ordinary pecking stay below the level likely to cause injury in a brain as small as a woodpecker's, although they would be dangerous for a brain the size of a human's. Their figures suggest that the birds would need to strike much harder before that safety margin began to disappear.

The study leaves room for the old features to matter, since the spongy bone may still help the skull resist damage over many years. But it changes the lesson engineers can take from the bird. A woodpecker shows how a small, stiff tool can strike safely, not how to cushion a large brain, and helmet designers may need to look elsewhere for ideas.

Every August my cousin Alvy and I spend two weeks at our grandmother's cottage near Ardmere, a village beside a wide, slow river. The cottage is small and old, and that summer it had a new resident. On the first morning, Alvy stepped out onto the porch with his toast and came straight back in, pale. Under the roof, just above the porch light, hung a grey ball the size of a melon, and wasps were drifting in and out of a hole near its bottom.

Alvy wanted it gone at once. He had been stung on the hand the summer before and had spent an afternoon with his arm in a bowl of ice. He found a long broom in the shed and announced that he would knock the nest into the river before breakfast was over. I was ready to help him. Our grandmother, who had been reading at the kitchen table, put down her book and asked us both to sit.

She told us that the wasps had been there since May and that she had been watching them all summer. They had built the nest themselves, she said, by chewing wood from the old fence into a kind of paper. Every morning she saw them carry green caterpillars back to it, and for the first time in years the cabbages in her garden had hardly a hole in them. "They feed those to their young," she explained. "I've had the best vegetables in the village."

Alvy pointed out that a wasp stings whoever is nearest, whatever garden it is protecting. My grandmother agreed. Knocking down a nest full of angry wasps, she said, was the surest way to be stung, and by more than one of them. Then she made an offer. The nest would last only until the cold weeks of autumn, when the colony would die out and the young queens would fly off to spend the winter somewhere else. Wasps build a fresh nest every year, so after that the old one could simply be taken down. If we could put up with them until then, she would make sure we stayed safe.

That afternoon we worked out the rules together. We moved the breakfast table from the porch to the shady side of the house, and we used the back door instead of the front one. My grandmother tied a red ribbon across the porch steps to mark the point where we had to stop. Alvy wrote the rules on a card in large letters and pinned it to the kitchen door, which I suspected was mostly so he could feel in charge.

By the second week, something had changed. Alvy, who had started the holiday armed with a broom, began sitting on the garden wall at a safe distance from the porch, watching the wasps come and go. He counted how many left the nest in a minute and wrote the numbers in a notebook. Nobody was stung that summer. On our last day he asked whether he could have the nest once it was empty, and my grandmother promised to post it to him in November, wrapped in newspaper. It arrived just before his birthday, as light as a dry leaf, and it now sits on a shelf above his bed.

Cato Derwin was born in 1934 in Cressley, a small mill town where most people worked long shifts and few had time for sport. As a teenager he ran everywhere, partly because the family could not afford a bicycle. By the age of twenty he was winning regional races over ten miles, and a newspaper in the nearest city called him the fastest young runner the county had produced.

Two years later, during a race on a wet road, he slipped and badly injured his left knee. Doctors told him that the knee would recover enough for daily life, but that serious racing was over. Derwin took a job as a postman, which kept him walking for six hours a day. He later said that those long walks gave him time to think about what running had meant to him.

On his rounds he noticed something that bothered him. Many of the men and women he delivered letters to were in their forties and fifties, and they often told him they felt tired and stiff. Several of them had played football or cycled when they were young, and had given up only when work and families filled their days. When he suggested they try running, almost all of them gave the same answer: running was for young athletes, and they were too old and too slow to start.

In the spring of 1961, Derwin put a small card in the window of the post office. It invited anyone to meet in Cressley Park at eight o'clock on Sunday morning. Only five people came. Instead of asking them to run around the park, he asked them to run for one minute and then walk for one minute, again and again, for half an hour. Experienced runners in the town laughed at the idea, and the local paper gave the group a nickname: the Sunday Shufflers.

Derwin ignored the jokes. He believed that the walking breaks were the whole point, because they let beginners finish a session feeling that they could do more. Week by week he made the running minutes slightly longer. By the end of the first year, the group had grown to more than sixty people, and several members who had started with one-minute runs completed a five-mile race in the city.

The Shufflers kept growing after that. A local doctor began suggesting the group to patients who wanted to become more active, and similar groups started in three neighbouring towns. Derwin led the Sunday sessions for almost thirty years without being paid, and by the end he knew the name of nearly every runner who came to the park. He never raced again, but when a reporter asked him in 1990 whether he missed competing, he answered that watching a grandmother finish her first race had pleased him more than any of his own victories.

Anyone who has started a new sport knows the feeling. The day after a first hike or a first long session in the gym, the legs feel fine, but the following morning climbing the stairs suddenly hurts, and even sitting down on a chair becomes uncomfortable. Scientists call this delayed onset muscle soreness, and the name describes its strangest feature: the pain usually begins several hours after the exercise, is strongest one to three days later, and then fades within about a week.

For much of the twentieth century, coaches and even textbooks offered a simple explanation. During hard exercise, muscles produce a substance called lactic acid, and it was widely believed that this acid stayed in the muscles and caused the pain. The idea seemed reasonable, because lactic acid really does build up during intense effort, and many athletes still repeat it today.

The explanation, however, does not fit the timing. Measurements show that lactic acid is cleared from the muscles within roughly an hour after exercise ends, long before the soreness appears. Something else had to be happening during the day or two that followed.

A clue came from comparing different kinds of movement. Muscles can work while shortening, as the front of the thigh does when a person climbs a hill, or while lengthening under a load, as the same muscle does when a person walks down the hill and has to brake at each step. In experiments, volunteers who walked or ran downhill reported far more soreness in the following days than those who went uphill, even though going uphill felt harder at the time and used more energy. The lengthening, braking kind of work turned out to be the kind most likely to cause soreness.

Most researchers now believe that this kind of work creates very small areas of damage inside the muscle fibres. Under a microscope, samples taken from sore muscles often show small signs of disruption in the fibres. Over the next day or two, the body responds by repairing them, and this repair process seems to make nearby nerve endings more sensitive, so that ordinary movements become painful. Scientists still debate the exact details, but the timing of the repair matches the timing of the pain far better than lactic acid ever did.

The research also explains a second puzzle. If people repeat the same exercise a week or two later, they usually feel much less sore, even if the second session is just as hard. The muscle seems to adapt quickly after the first experience, which is why trainers advise beginners to start gently and build up over several weeks. For the same reason, soreness is a poor measure of a good workout: an experienced runner may train very hard and feel almost nothing the next day.

Two hundred years ago, the shops along the main street of Gelmouth, a busy market town, looked almost exactly like the houses beside them. Each shop front had one or two ordinary windows made of many small panes, each about the size of a book, held together by strips of wood or lead. The glass was thick and slightly green, and it bent the light, so a person standing in the street saw only dim shapes inside. To find out what a shop sold, you had to know already, or you had to open the door and ask.

At that time, glass was made by hand. A worker blew a large bubble of hot glass and then spun or cut it into flat pieces, and the method could only produce small sheets of good quality. Large panes often cracked as they cooled, and in some countries glass was also taxed, so a big window was a luxury that few shopkeepers could afford. Shopping in Gelmouth was therefore a matter of trust and habit. People bought their bread, cloth and nails from the same families their parents had used, and a stranger rarely walked into a shop just to look.

In the middle of the nineteenth century, new methods made it possible to produce large, flat sheets of clear glass at a much lower price. The first Gelmouth shop to use one was a draper's owned by Eben Garrod, who sold cloth and ribbons. In 1852 he replaced his old front with a single pane roughly two metres wide. Neighbours called it a waste of money and predicted that it would break in the first winter storm. Instead, it became the most talked-about object in the town.

What Garrod did next mattered even more than the glass itself. Behind the window he built a low platform and arranged his brightest fabrics on it, changing the display every week. On market days, families who had never bought anything from him stopped to look, and some came inside to ask about prices. Within a year his sales had roughly doubled, and the other shopkeepers on the street began to save for windows of their own.

The change spread surprisingly fast. By about 1880, nearly every shop on the main street had a large window, and the shopkeepers competed to make their displays the most attractive. A baker named Gilbert Ebbs piled his loaves into the shape of the town hall, and a toy seller put a small moving train in her window. For the first time, people walked along the street in the evening simply to enjoy the windows, a habit that the people of Gelmouth called "taking the glass." Shopkeepers soon discovered that a window lit by gas lamps after dark could attract more customers than the busiest market morning.

The new windows had critics as well. Some older customers complained that shopping had become a show and that prices rose to pay for the glass and the lamps. Small shops that were unable to buy a large window sometimes lost trade to their richer neighbours. Yet the windows changed something lasting about the town: a shop stopped being a private room that only regular customers entered and became a public space that invited anyone in the street to look first and decide later.

My grandmother has run a small sewing shop near the market square in Elmwick for almost forty years. She sells thread, buttons, zips, needles and fabric, and the walls are covered with drawers, each with a label in her neat handwriting. When I was a child, the shop seemed to me like the most crowded place in the world. On a Saturday you could hardly reach the counter.

By the time I turned sixteen, those busy Saturdays had gone. Big stores on the edge of town sold cheaper fabric, and many people bought buttons and thread online with a single click. Some weeks my grandmother took in less money than she paid in rent. One evening, while I was helping her count the money in the till, she told me quietly that she might have to close the shop by the end of the year.

I was sure I knew the answer. The shop needed a website. I spent most of my summer holiday photographing buttons and writing descriptions, and in September we opened an online store. For a few weeks I checked it every hour. In that time we sold eleven packets of needles, three zips and one pair of scissors. The postage and the website fee cost more than we earned, and the problem was simple: anyone could find the same buttons more cheaply on bigger sites.

The real answer came from somewhere I had ignored. Every few days, someone walked into the shop holding a torn coat or a pair of trousers that needed shortening and asked my grandmother whether she knew anyone who could fix it. She always did the job herself, usually for almost nothing, because she thought of it as a favour. One afternoon a young man came in with a jacket that had lost a button, and while she sewed on a new one, he asked whether she ever taught people to do it themselves.

That question changed the shop. In October my grandmother started a mending class on Thursday evenings, for six people around the big table at the back. It filled within two days. She taught people to sew on buttons, fix hems and patch elbows, and at the end of every class almost everyone bought the thread, needles and buttons they needed for their own repairs at home. Soon she added a second evening, and then a Saturday morning class for teenagers.

A year later, the shop is still open. The classes themselves earn only a modest amount, but the students keep coming back for supplies, and many of them bring friends. The website still exists, though I hardly look at it. What I learned is that I had been trying to make the shop more like the big stores, when the thing people wanted was the one thing the big stores could never offer: someone who could help them make and mend things with their own hands.

passage:
On a clear spring night, a fruit farmer may do something that looks completely backwards. As the temperature falls toward freezing, the farmer turns on sprinklers and covers the trees in water. By sunrise, every branch and blossom is wrapped in ice, hanging in glassy drops. Yet when the ice melts, the flowers underneath are often healthy, while blossoms on unsprayed trees nearby have turned brown and died.

The danger comes from timing. Many fruit trees flower early in spring, when warm days can still be followed by cold nights. An open blossom is delicate: depending on the type of fruit and how far the flower has opened, a few hours at around two or three degrees below freezing can kill the tiny parts that would later become fruit. One bad night can destroy most of a season's harvest before a single fruit has formed.

The sprinklers work because of a fact about water that surprises many people: when water freezes, it gives off heat. Turning liquid water into ice means removing energy from it, and that energy has to go somewhere. On a sprayed tree, much of it goes into the bud. As long as fresh water keeps arriving and freezing, the thin mix of water and ice around each blossom stays at about zero degrees Celsius, the freezing point, even if the air around the tree is several degrees colder. The ice, in other words, acts less like a freezer than like a heater set to exactly zero.

The method has strict rules, however. The water must keep coming all night, and the sprinklers must stay on after sunrise until the ice begins to melt and slide off. This is the part beginners often get wrong. If the spraying stops too early, the thin layer of water on the ice begins to evaporate, and evaporation draws heat out of the bud, about seven times as much heat for each gram of water as freezing releases. A farmer who switches off at dawn to save water can lose more blossoms than a neighbour who never sprayed at all.

There are other costs too. Spraying a large orchard through a cold night uses an enormous amount of water, which many farms cannot afford in a dry year. The ice is also heavy, and on older trees a thick coat can snap branches. For these reasons, some growers prefer large fans on tall poles. On calm, frosty nights, the air a few metres above the ground is often warmer than the air at the bottom, and the fans push that warmer air down among the trees. Fans use far less water, but they help only when such a warm layer exists.

Even so, for many fruit growers the sprinkler remains the most reliable defence against a spring frost. It is one of the few cases in farming where the answer to cold is, quite literally, more ice.

For most of the nineteenth century, very few houses in the farming village of Inchmere had an oven of their own. A brick oven large enough to bake bread needs a great deal of wood to heat, and most families could spare little room and even less fuel. Instead, the whole village shared a single oven, which stood in a low stone building beside the mill.

The oven belonged to the miller's family, and for over forty years it was run by a woman named Hettie Jessop. Each morning she lit a fire inside it before dawn, raked out the ashes once the bricks were hot, and opened the door to customers at seven. Families mixed their dough at home and carried it to her on wooden boards. To tell the loaves apart, each household pressed its own sign into the top of the dough: a cross, a star, a set of dots. In return for her work, Hettie kept a small piece of every family's dough, which she baked and sold to travellers.

Because one fire baked bread for nearly sixty households, the system used far less wood than separate ovens would have. It also shaped the week. Bread was baked on Tuesdays and Fridays, and on those mornings the oven house became the busiest place in Inchmere. While their loaves baked, people waited on benches outside and exchanged news: who was ill, whose cow had calved, what prices the market town was paying for wheat. A visiting teacher later wrote that she learned more about the village in one baking morning than in a month of church services.

The change came with the railway. When a line reached the market town of Jandrel in 1879, factory-made iron stoves began to arrive at prices ordinary families could afford. An iron stove burned coal, heated a kitchen in winter and baked a loaf whenever its owner chose. Within fifteen years, roughly two thirds of Inchmere's households had one.

Hettie's customers slowly disappeared. By 1895 she was baking for fewer than twenty families, and the oven was lit only on Fridays. She tried to make up the difference by baking more bread of her own to sell, but the travellers who had once bought it now came through on the train and seldom stopped. When she retired in 1901, nobody took her place, and the oven house was later turned into a storeroom for the mill.

Older villagers complained for years afterwards that Inchmere had become a quieter, lonelier place. News that once spread in a single morning now took days, if it arrived at all. The stoves had saved families the walk to the mill, but they had also removed the one ordinary reason everyone had to meet.

When a car turns a corner, its outside wheels must travel farther than its inside wheels. A car solves this with a set of gears that lets each wheel turn at its own speed. The wheels of a train cannot do this. Each pair is fixed to one solid steel bar called an axle, so both wheels always turn together.

So how does a train get around a bend? The answer is in the shape of its wheels. The part of a train wheel that touches the rail is not flat. It is shaped like a slice of a cone, slightly wider near the inside of the wheel and narrower toward the outside.

On a curve, the train drifts a little toward the outside of the bend. This makes the outer wheel roll on its wider part and the inner wheel roll on its narrower part. In one full turn, a wide circle covers more ground than a narrow one, so the outer wheel travels farther even though both wheels turn at the same rate.

The same shape also keeps a train centred on straight track. If the train slips to one side, the wheels on that side roll on their wider part and steer it back toward the middle. Each wheel also has a raised rim on its inner edge, but this is mainly a safety feature for sharp curves. On most track, the cone shape does the steering.

In the 1830s the town of Lunford, a busy river port of about twelve thousand people, had grown too long for comfortable walking. Its docks lay at the southern end, its market and offices at the northern end, and the workers who lived near one often had to reach the other. A private carriage was far beyond the means of a dock labourer or a shop assistant, so most people simply walked, sometimes for an hour in each direction.

In 1834 a carpenter named Kester Larkham built a long wooden carriage with benches along both sides, hitched it to two horses, and began driving it up and down Kemble Street, the road that joined the two ends of town. Anyone could ride for a penny. Within a month his vehicle was carrying several hundred passengers a day, and Larkham had ordered a second one.

Success quickly created a problem. Larkham's drivers stopped wherever someone raised a hand, so a journey that should have taken twenty minutes could stretch to fifty. Regular riders complained that they could never predict when they would arrive at work, and some went back to walking. Larkham's answer was to paint a dozen wooden posts bright green and set them along Kemble Street at roughly equal distances. From then on, the carriages would halt only at a post, and a printed card in every carriage listed the times at which each post would be reached.

Not everyone welcomed the posts. Several shopkeepers on Kemble Street had enjoyed having customers step down directly outside their doors, and they argued that a stop in front of a rival's window would ruin them. Lisbet Umber, who sold hats near the middle of the street, collected the names of forty traders on a letter asking the town council to remove the posts. The council, which had little power over a private business, declined to act, but it suggested that Larkham meet the traders himself.

The meeting produced a compromise that pleased few people at first. Larkham kept his posts but agreed to move three of them so that each stood between two shops rather than in front of one. Within a year, however, the traders had changed their minds. Passengers waiting at a post had several minutes to fill, and they spent them looking into the nearest windows. The shops closest to the green posts did noticeably better than before, and by 1840 Umber herself was paying Larkham a small fee each year to have a post placed outside her door.

Larkham's green posts are often described as the first fixed stops in the region. Whether or not that is true, they show how quickly a convenience can become part of daily life: within a generation, the people of Lunford gave directions by them, telling visitors to walk two posts north of the bridge or to wait at the fifth post.

From there it is a five-minute walk along the river, and the museum is on the corner. I drove the 12 for nineteen years, long before you were born."

Una had known, in a general way, that her grandfather had once worked on the trams. It was one of those family facts that are mentioned at birthdays and then forgotten. She had never imagined that the city's lines might still be stored in his head, stop by stop, like a song he had learned as a child.

They took the 12. Her grandfather named each stop a second before the recorded voice did, and twice he told her about buildings that were no longer there: a cinema where a supermarket now stood, and a bakery that had sold bread shaped like horseshoes. At the fish market he set off along the river so quickly that she had to hurry to keep up.

The exhibition filled two rooms. Near the end of the second, Konrad stopped in front of a large black-and-white photograph of a tram crossing a bridge in heavy snow. He leaned so close that his nose almost touched the glass, and then he asked Una to read him the small card beside it. On a freezing morning, many people discover a small but annoying fact about their phones. With their gloves on, they tap the screen again and again, and the phone ignores every tap. It has not frozen, and the gloves may be quite thin. The screen is simply unable to notice them, and the reason lies in how most modern touchscreens are built.

Most phones and tablets today use what engineers call a capacitive screen. Under the glass lies a fine grid of transparent material that conducts electricity, and the phone keeps a weak electric field across it. A human finger is a reasonably good conductor, because the body contains a great deal of salty water. When a fingertip comes close to the glass, it disturbs the field at that point, and the phone measures exactly where the change has happened. Wool, leather and most other glove materials are poor conductors, so the field stays almost the same and the screen behaves as if nothing has touched it.

Touchscreens did not always work this way. Many earlier devices, such as ticket machines and the first handheld computers, used resistive screens. These were made of two flexible sheets separated by a very thin gap. Pressing the top sheet pushed it against the lower one, and the device detected the point where they met. Because it responded to pressure alone, a resistive screen worked with a fingernail, a plastic pen or a thick winter glove. Its weaknesses were that it needed a firm push, the extra layers made the picture slightly duller, and it usually recognised only one point of contact at a time.

Phone makers began switching to capacitive screens in large numbers in the late 2000s. What attracted them was a screen that reacted to the lightest touch and could follow two fingers at once, so that a user could spread them apart to enlarge a photo or a map. The cost of this change was hardly visible in a warm shop. A screen that senses electric charge responds only to objects that conduct electricity, and a gloved hand in winter is not one of them.

Manufacturers and users have found several ways around the problem. Some winter gloves now have threads coated with silver or copper sewn into the fingertips, which carry the effect of the finger through the fabric. A simple stylus designed for these screens has a soft tip made of conductive rubber, and the tip is roughly as wide as a fingertip, because a very narrow point changes the field too little to be detected. Some phones also include a setting that makes the screen more sensitive, so that it can find a finger through a thin glove, although this setting can make accidental touches more common.

The same physics explains a less familiar problem. Rainwater conducts electricity well enough that a phone used in heavy rain may react to drops on the glass as if they were fingers, opening apps or typing letters on its own. In other words, the feature that makes these screens so pleasant to use is also the source of their strangest failures: they do not really feel a touch at all, only the electrical presence of something that behaves like skin.

Ottilie Mendrell was born in Netherholt, a mountain village whose only road ran down a narrow valley to the market town of Ollendale, about thirty kilometres away. Her father repaired clocks, and as a girl she spent long evenings at his bench, learning how small parts could be made to work together. At sixteen she built an oil lamp that put itself out when its fuel ran low, and the village talked about it for weeks.

Netherholt's problem was distance. A message to Ollendale had to be carried on horseback, which took most of a day on the steep road, and in winter the road could be blocked by snow for a week or more. Ottilie had read about armies that sent signals with flashes of sunlight, and she knew that the church tower in Ollendale could be seen from the hill above her village on clear days. In the spring of her twentieth year, she proposed placing a large mirror at each end, so that the two places could exchange messages by flashing sunlight across the valley in a simple code of long and short flashes.

The village council was unimpressed. Its oldest member, Nevin Osterfeld, argued that a mirror would be useless at night or under cloud, which was true, and that the money would be better spent on widening the road. Others simply laughed at the idea of talking with sunshine. Ottilie replied that a storm would close even a wider road, while the sky usually cleared within a day or two. After a long debate, the council gave her a small sum, about half of what she had asked for.

With half the money, Ottilie could afford only one large mirror, so she placed it on the hill above Netherholt and, for the first months, used a much smaller mirror lent by the church in Ollendale. She spent the summer training two boys from each place to send and read the code. The first messages were short and slow, and a cloud passing at the wrong moment could ruin a whole sentence, but by autumn the two stations could exchange a simple message in less than an hour.

The real test came that winter. In January a heavy snowfall closed the road for nine days, and on the third day a child in Netherholt fell seriously ill. On the first clear morning, the hill station flashed a request for a doctor, and Ollendale replied within the hour that one would set out on skis. He arrived the next afternoon, and the child recovered. After that, the council paid for a second large mirror without any argument, and Nevin Osterfeld himself climbed the hill to watch the first message sent with it.

The mirrors served the two places for about fourteen years, until a telephone line was finally strung along the valley road. Ottilie welcomed it. By then she was running a small workshop in Netherholt that repaired sewing machines and farm tools, and she said the telephone did the job better, since it worked at night. When people later asked whether she was sad to see her mirrors taken down, she answered that she had never cared about the mirrors themselves, only about the messages.

When the Quorndale Museum opened in 1851, it held the collection of a wealthy cloth merchant, Roderick Paskin, who had spent forty years buying shells, coins, old maps and stuffed birds from dealers abroad. His will left the objects and a handsome stone building to the town, together with a set of rules. The museum would open from ten until four, Monday to Saturday, and every visitor had to bring a letter from a respected citizen.

For more than twenty years these rules decided who saw the collection. The town's mills ran from six in the morning until six at night, six days a week, so the people who made up most of Quorndale had little spare time during opening hours. Few of them, moreover, knew anyone who could write the required letter. The visitors' book from the 1860s shows about two thousand names a year, almost all of them doctors, lawyers, merchants and their families.

The change began with a new keeper, Peregrine Rusby, appointed in 1873. Rusby had grown up in a mill family himself, and he argued that a gift to the town ought to be open to the whole town. He asked the trustees to drop the letter rule and to open the doors on Sunday afternoons, the only hours most workers could call their own. The trustees were divided. Some feared that crowds would break the glass display cases or carry off small coins. The town's minister, Rufus Pendle, objected for a different reason: Sunday, he said, was a day for church and rest, and a museum open on that day would encourage people to treat it like any other.

In the end the trustees agreed to a trial of one year, and the results surprised both sides. Sunday visitors numbered about fourteen thousand that year, seven times the old total. Many arrived in family groups straight from the midday meal, and on wet afternoons the keeper had to admit them fifty at a time. His report for the year noted a single broken pane of glass, caused by a child who slipped on the stairs. Weekday visitors, the merchants and professionals who had always come, kept coming at about the same rate. Pendle went on preaching against Sunday opening for several years, but attendance at his own services showed little change.

The most lasting effect was one that nobody had planned. Many of the new visitors began bringing objects of their own: a weaver's shuttle more than a century old, fossils split from the stone of the local quarry, a wooden doll carved by a soldier's widow. Rusby accepted almost everything, labelled each piece with the giver's name, and gave the gifts a room of their own. By 1890 that room had grown into three, and guidebooks were describing the Quorndale Museum less as a merchant's cabinet of foreign curiosities than as a record of the town itself.

A song stored on a music CD takes up a surprising amount of space. Each second of stereo sound is described by roughly 1.4 million bits of data, so a three-minute song needs about 30 megabytes. In the early 1990s, when most home computers had small hard drives and slow internet connections, sending a single song to a friend could take hours. Engineers wanted a way to make music files much smaller while keeping them pleasant to listen to.

The obvious approaches were to throw away information at random or to record the sound less precisely everywhere, but both made the music sound rough. The successful approach started from a different question: which parts of a sound does a listener actually hear? The answer comes from the scientific study of hearing, known as psychoacoustics. Human ears are most sensitive to middle pitches, roughly those of speech, and much less sensitive to very low and very high ones. A quiet sound at the edges of that range can therefore be dropped with little effect.

More important is an effect called masking. When a loud sound and a quiet sound occur at the same moment and at similar pitches, the loud one hides the quiet one, and the ear simply does not register it. A soft flute note played during a crash of cymbals, for example, may be completely covered. Masking also works for a short moment in time: just after a loud sound, nearby quieter sounds are harder to hear.

An encoder, the program that creates the smaller file, uses these facts. It splits each short slice of music into many narrow bands of pitch and estimates, band by band, how much of the sound will be masked. Bands that a listener would notice receive plenty of data, while bands that are hidden receive little or none. At a common setting of 128 thousand bits per second, the result is about one-eleventh the size of the original, so the three-minute song shrinks to roughly 3 megabytes. When the song is played, a decoder on the listener's computer rebuilds the sound from this smaller description.

The method has a price. The removed information is gone for good, so the original recording can be rebuilt from the smaller file only approximately. Engineers tested their encoders by asking trained listeners to compare compressed and uncompressed versions of the same music, and for most recordings at the common setting, many listeners were unable to tell them apart reliably. Certain sounds, however, gave the trick away. Sharp, sudden noises such as castanets could be preceded by a faint smear, because the encoder had spread its errors across a stretch of time that began before the sound itself. Recordings like these were used again and again to improve later versions.

In the 1800s, the hill town of Tavenor depended on one business: its slate quarry. Slate is a dark gray rock that splits into thin, flat sheets. Workers cut large blocks from the hillside and then split them by hand with a hammer and chisel.

Most of Tavenor's slate became roof tiles. Builders liked it because it kept out rain and lasted far longer than wood or clay. The thinnest, smoothest sheets went to a small workshop in town, where they were set in wooden frames and sold to schools as writing slates. passage:
Anyone who lives a few kilometres from a railway line may have noticed something odd. During the day, the trains pass almost unheard. On a still, clear night, the same trains seem to rumble right past the bedroom window, and a dog barking on a distant farm can sound as if it were in the garden. The trains make the same noise at both times, and the dog is just as far away. The difference lies in the air itself.

Sound is a wave of pressure that travels through the air, and its speed depends partly on the air's temperature. Sound moves a little faster in warm air than in cold air: at about 20 degrees Celsius it covers roughly 343 metres per second, while near freezing it manages about 331. That small gap matters, because when a sound wave passes from air of one temperature into air of another, it changes direction slightly. Scientists call this bending refraction, and the wave always turns toward the cooler, slower air.

On a sunny afternoon, the ground heats up and warms the air just above it, so the air is usually warmest near the surface and cooler higher up. A sound made near the ground therefore curves upward, away from listeners, and much of its energy is lost to the sky. A person some distance away may hear only a faint version of it, or nothing at all, because they are standing in what researchers call a shadow zone.

After sunset on a clear, calm night, the pattern often reverses. The ground gives off its heat quickly into the open sky, and it chills the thin layer of air resting on it. For a few hours, cool air may lie beneath warmer air, an arrangement known as a temperature inversion. Sound that starts to travel upward now curves back down toward the ground. Instead of escaping, it is guided along the surface, and it can reach listeners several kilometres away more strongly than it would by day.

Wind adds a second effect. It usually blows faster a little above the ground than at the surface, where trees, buildings and the ground itself slow it down. As a result, sound travelling with the wind tends to bend downward, while sound travelling against it bends upward. This is why the bells of a town, or the crowd at a stadium, may be clear on one side and hard to hear on the other. On a windy night, the moving air also stirs the layers together, which can spoil an inversion.

These effects are more than a curiosity. Engineers planning new airports, wind farms and factories now study local weather records before predicting how far noise will spread, because a plan based only on daytime measurements can underestimate what neighbours will hear at night. For the people near the railway, the explanation offers a small comfort: the trains themselves are as loud as they always were, and it is the night air that brings them closer.

passage:
Tova had spent the whole autumn learning rocks by their colour. She kept a box of forty samples under her bed, and every evening she tipped them onto the carpet and named them as fast as she could: pink feldspar, white quartz, black hematite, green olivine. By November she could name all forty in under two minutes, and she was sure that the regional mineral contest in Selwyn would be easy. Her older brother timed her each evening with a stopwatch from the kitchen drawer.

Her partner, Zeke, worked much more slowly. He carried a small square of white tile, a steel nail and a magnifying glass, and he would scratch and rub a sample for a full minute before writing anything down. Tova found it hard to watch. On the bus to Selwyn she told him, as kindly as she could, that the contest gave each pair only thirty minutes for twenty samples. Zeke only nodded and went on polishing his tile with his sleeve.

The contest room was a science laboratory with long black tables. On each table stood a numbered tray, and the organisers had chosen the samples with care. A bell would ring when the thirty minutes were over. Some were wet. Some were coated in dust. Several were pieces Tova had never seen in that colour: a quartz crystal stained brownish-yellow, a dull grey lump that turned out to be hematite, a feldspar so pale it was almost white.

For the first ten minutes Tova wrote quickly and confidently. Then she reached sample eleven, which looked exactly like the grey lump before it, and she realised she had no idea which of the two was hematite. The clock on the wall showed twenty minutes left. She glanced across at Zeke. He had rubbed sample ten across his tile, and it had left a reddish-brown line. "Hematite always streaks red-brown," he whispered, "whatever colour the outside is." Sample eleven left a dark grey streak.

Tova looked back at her sheet. Of the ten samples she had already named, she now doubted four. She picked up the brownish crystal and drew it across the glass of a spare slide. It cut a clean line, which calcite would never do. It was quartz after all. With eight minutes left, she and Zeke worked through the rest of the tray together, she describing each sample's colour and shape, he testing each guess before either of them wrote it down.

They finished with seconds to spare and came third out of fourteen schools. On the bus home, Tova found the slide still in her pocket. She kept it. That week she bought a white tile of her own, and when she tipped the forty samples onto the carpet again, she left the stopwatch in the drawer and took her time over each one.
